headline: Connecticut prison-cost law leaves former inmates and families facing debt claims
dek: A Connecticut Mirror investigation found the state collected about $21 million from 2020 through mid-2026 under a law that bills people for incarceration costs and can reach inheritances, settlements and other assets.
body: Connecticut's decades-old prison-cost law is leaving some formerly incarcerated people and their families with large claims years after release, according to a Connecticut Mirror investigation published Sept. 27.

The report found that the state collected about $21 million from 2020 through mid-2026 after reviewing hundreds of cases and interviewing more than a dozen people. The Connecticut Department of Correction can assess the unreimbursed cost of a person's incarceration, while the Department of Administrative Services handles collections.

Connecticut's current law allows the state to make a claim against an inmate's property, subject to exemptions. A related provision permits liens on certain lawsuit proceeds and inheritances received within 20 years of release, with the claim generally limited to the incarceration cost or half of the proceeds, whichever is less.

The investigation found that the daily rate has reached $347, enough to create a bill of nearly $127,000 for a year in prison. The state's own Department of Correction FAQ says collections can involve decedent estates and money or assets received from lawsuits, personal-injury insurance claims or inheritances.

The reporting examined the case of a North Branford woman whose late husband's prison-cost claim became part of an estate dispute and contributed to the loss of the home they had shared. Connecticut officials say the collection system is authorized by state law; the investigation has renewed attention on how those claims affect reentry, survivors and families.
author: NorthEast News Desk
